subject: mathematics
question_text: In triangle ABC, O is the circumcentre and H is the orthocentre. Show that OA + OB + OC = OH.

mark_split.label: Set up the point P with OP = OA + OB + OC
Show AP is perpendicular to BC
Show BP is perpendicular to CA
Conclude that P is the orthocentre H

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.64, chapter 6 ADDITION OF VECTORS, Short Answer question 5(i). Only the question was taken — the solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work, see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. METHOD CHOICE RECORDED: the proof authored here is self-contained and uses vector ADDITION only — it names the point P with OP = OA + OB + OC and shows P lies on two altitudes, using the midpoint relation OB + OC = 2 OD and the fact that the median of an isosceles triangle is perpendicular to its base. It deliberately does NOT quote the Euler line result (that O, the centroid and H are collinear with OH = 3 OG), because that result is normally derived FROM this one, and it does not use the dot product, which belongs to the next chapter. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 split rewards the set-up, each of the two perpendicularity arguments, and the closing statement that two altitudes meet only at the orthocentre. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern; Addition of Vectors has no Section C slot on the paper, so the unit is SAQ and VSAQ only. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say what point you name first and what you then have to show about it.

steps.label: Name the point P
steps.margin_note: First mark. Do not work towards H directly. Give the sum OA + OB + OC a name, P, and then prove P is the orthocentre. Also write down what circumcentre means, because the equal radii are used twice below.
steps.memory_tip: Name the sum P first, then prove P is H. Circumcentre means the three distances |OA|, |OB|, |OC| are equal.
lines: O is the circumcentre of triangle ABC, so
OA, OB, OC are radii of one circle:
|OA| = |OB| = |OC|.
Let P be the point given by
OP = OA + OB + OC.   ……(1)
We show that P is the orthocentre H.

recall.must_convey: That the sum OA + OB + OC is named as the position vector of a point P, and that the plan is to prove P is the orthocentre, using |OA| = |OB| = |OC|.
accept: let P be the point whose position vector from O is OA plus OB plus OC
name the sum as a point P and then show P is the orthocentre
O is the circumcentre so the three distances OA OB and OC are equal
sum ni P ani peru petti, P ye orthocentre ani prove chestam
start by writing that the circumradii are all equal

steps.why: The orthocentre is defined as the point where the altitudes meet, so it cannot be computed directly. Naming a candidate point and checking it against that definition is the only route open.
common_mistakes: Trying to write OH down at the start, when H has no formula yet.
Forgetting that circumcentre means equal distances, which is the only property of O the proof uses.

steps.label: Show AP is perpendicular to BC
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two facts meet here: the midpoint rule turns OB + OC into 2 OD, and the isosceles triangle OBC has its median OD at right angles to BC. Together they put P on the altitude from A.
steps.memory_tip: OB + OC = 2 OD, and OD is the median of the isosceles triangle OBC, so OD is at right angles to BC.
lines: Let D be the midpoint of BC.
Then OB + OC = 2 OD.   ……(2)
From (1) and (2),
AP = OP − OA = OB + OC = 2 OD
|OB| = |OC|, so triangle OBC is isosceles
and its median OD is at right angles to BC.
AP is parallel to OD, so AP ⊥ BC.
∴ P lies on the altitude through A.

recall.must_convey: That AP = OP − OA = OB + OC = 2 OD, and that OD is perpendicular to BC because triangle OBC is isosceles, so AP is perpendicular to BC.
accept: AP equals OB plus OC which is twice OD where D is the midpoint of BC
triangle OBC is isosceles so the median OD is perpendicular to BC
AP is parallel to OD so AP is perpendicular to BC
OB plus OC equals two OD, D ante BC midpoint
so P lies on the altitude from A

steps.why: An altitude is the line through a vertex at right angles to the opposite side. Showing AP is at right angles to BC is exactly the statement that P sits somewhere on the altitude drawn from A.
common_mistakes: Writing OB + OC = OD and losing the factor 2.
Claiming OD ⊥ BC without saying that |OB| = |OC| makes triangle OBC isosceles.

steps.label: Show BP is perpendicular to CA
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The same argument again, one vertex along. Repeat it in full rather than writing "similarly" — the examiner is paying for the second altitude, and two altitudes are what pin the point down.
steps.memory_tip: Repeat the same three lines at B: midpoint E of CA, OC + OA = 2 OE, and OE at right angles to CA.
lines: Let E be the midpoint of CA.
Then OC + OA = 2 OE.
From (1),
BP = OP − OB = OC + OA = 2 OE
|OC| = |OA|, so triangle OCA is isosceles
and its median OE is at right angles to CA.
BP is parallel to OE, so BP ⊥ CA.
∴ P lies on the altitude through B.

recall.must_convey: That the same argument at B gives BP = OC + OA = 2 OE with OE perpendicular to CA, so P lies on the altitude through B as well.
accept: do the same at B with E the midpoint of CA
BP equals OC plus OA which is twice OE and OE is perpendicular to CA
triangle OCA is isosceles so its median OE is at right angles to CA
same argument B daggara repeat cheste BP perpendicular to CA
so P lies on the second altitude too

steps.why: One altitude is a whole line of points, so it cannot identify P. A second altitude cuts that line at a single point, and that point is the one the definition of the orthocentre names.
common_mistakes: Taking E as the midpoint of AB instead of CA, so the vectors no longer match BP.
Writing only "similarly" and showing no working for the second altitude.

steps.label: Conclude that P is H
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Two altitudes meet at exactly one point, and by definition that point is the orthocentre. Say that sentence before writing the boxed line, or the proof stops one step short.
steps.memory_tip: Two altitudes meet at one point only, and that point is the orthocentre by definition.
lines: P lies on the altitude through A and on the
altitude through B.
Two altitudes meet at one point only, and
that point is the orthocentre H.
So P = H, and from (1),

recall.must_convey: That P lies on two altitudes, that two altitudes meet only at the orthocentre, so P = H and OA + OB + OC = OH.
accept: P is on two altitudes so P must be the orthocentre
two altitudes meet at only one point which is H so P equals H
therefore OA plus OB plus OC equals OH
rendu altitudes okka point daggare kalustayi, adi orthocentre
since P is H the sum of the three vectors is OH

steps.why: The three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent, and their common point is the orthocentre. That theorem is what lets a point proved to lie on two altitudes be named H. Everything before this step was about the vectors; this step turns it into the statement the question asked for.
common_mistakes: Stopping after the second altitude without saying P = H.
Checking only one altitude, which leaves P anywhere on that line.
